paragraphs.text:
[Of Cyril,] Archbishop of [?]: On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten, and that Christ is One and Lord.

A. Do you think that our discussion of the divinity of the Only-begotten has been well and adequately measured out and worked through? [?] Seven [?] says, the whole of the book [?]

B. I would rightly praise it as correct and finely polished.

A. Then, leaving these matters and dwelling on them no longer, will you have us speak about the incarnation of the Only-begotten, and whatever the mystery connected with it may be, trying to set it out as clearly as we can — at least as far as is possible for those who see in a mirror and in a riddle and know in part, according to the measure of the gift of the Spirit's supply, as the divine Paul writes?

B. Excellently said. "For no one says 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit, and no one says 'Jesus is accursed' except in Beelzebul." But since you seem willing to step into the dust of this contest too, and to endure a labor so [?] and so hard to bear, you would perhaps benefit others, and me before the rest. For I would most gladly learn the exact and unadulterated account of Christ, free from every fault. Some are drunk on various opinions, and twist into something unseemly what has been prophetically spoken about him by the New and the older Scripture.

A. Nothing, my friend, is [?] to them, but they leap most readily into the pit of Hades, as it is written, and into the snare of death, understanding neither what they say nor what they so confidently affirm. But what are each one's babblings and solemn little myths? Would you tell me, noble sir?

B. Certainly. Some have dared to declare that the Word from God appeared as a man, but not that he actually bore the flesh from the Virgin. They falsely ascribe to the mystery mere appearance. Others again, pretending to blush at seeming to worship a man, and refusing to crown the flesh from the earth with the highest glories, and out of sheer ignorance, sick with a bastard and corrupted piety, say that [the Word] was changed into the nature of flesh. The wretches laugh broadly at Emmanuel's birth from the Virgin, and ascribe [?] to so excellent and God-befitting a dispensation. Others again have believed that God the Word, coeternal with the Father, is late-born, and [?]: "If [he is] [?], as they say, he is not eternal; if eternal, as we say, he is not later." And a little after: "For among things that come into being, the before and [?]"

On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten.

— that he was called into existence only at the time when he also received the beginning of his birth according to the flesh. And there are some who have impiously reached such a pitch of madness that they even say [?] the Word from God [?], but that a mere word, understood only as something uttered, came to be in a man. [?] these [?]. Others again think that the Only-begotten truly became man, and they believe that he came to be in flesh, but not that he also fully ensouled the flesh he assumed with a rational soul possessing a mind like ours, uniting [?], as they suppose. [Speaking of] the Word from God and the temple from the holy Virgin, they say that the Word dwelt in it and made the assumed body his own, but that he himself filled the place of the rational and intellectual [soul]. Others again champion the opposite of these opinions and set themselves against such thinking. They affirm that the Word of God, and a rational soul and a body — that is, simply a complete humanity — came together and were interwoven, [so as to make] Emmanuel; yet they have not kept their doctrine about him wholly sound and blameless. For they divide the one Christ into two, and as if driving a thick cleft between them, they present each part as all but standing apart from the other. They insist that the one born of the Virgin, perfectly a man, is one, and the Word from God the Father is another. They do not merely distinguish what the nature of the Word is and what the nature of the flesh is, nor are they content to dwell only on the differences in this respect — for then they would not miss the true sense, since the nature of flesh and that of God are not the same. Rather, they set the one apart by himself as a man, and call the other, as God, Son by nature and in truth. [?] they want to be Christians, and indeed, writing some little treatises on this subject, they have dared to say in these very words: "For the Word from God the Father is Son by nature and in truth. [?] homonymously with [?]." And after other things again: "God's Word is not flesh, but has assumed a man. For the Only-begotten is primarily and in his own right Son of God, [the Father?], the Creator of all; but the man he assumed [?], because of the one who assumed him, who is truly Son of God, bears the name homonymously with him. For the words 'No one knows the Son except the Father' indicate the one who is Son from the Father by nature and in truth. But what was said by Gabriel — 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God; and behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus' — applies to the man." That is what they say. But let us not think in this way. For the argument of the heterodox will in no way persuade us to abandon the straight track and walk another. So carry out what you have in mind, and try to tell me, for I am ready to listen and to learn as fully as possible what is genuine.

A. How heavy the matter is, and how utterly hard to carry the burden! Do you not know, my friend, that if someone chose to make a long discourse on each point, and [Patrologia Graeca 75.]
a sustained examination, he would barely accomplish it, after spending no small amount of time and enduring heavy and inescapable sweat?

A. Then let us, if you agree, set aside [?] and speak very briefly, giving each only a little examination. Come, let us say, and to the Docetists before the others: "You are in error, not knowing the Scriptures," nor indeed the great mystery of godliness, that is, Christ, "who was manifested in the flesh, vindicated in the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory." I think that those who hold the opposite must either pass the more shameful verdict on the men of old and call liars the teachers of the mysteries to the whole world, to whom Christ himself said, "Go, make disciples of all nations"; or else, if they shudder to do this, they must choose to think rightly about Christ, bid farewell to their own ignorance, cling tightly to the sacred Scriptures, and, treading the unerring path of the saints, go on to the truth itself. For what would the great mystery be, other than the Word himself from God the Father, who was manifested in the flesh? For he was born through the holy Virgin, taking the form of a servant. And he was seen also by angels, who honor him at his birth: "Glory," they say, "to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." And indeed, announcing to the shepherds God the Word in the flesh for our sake, they say, "Behold, a Savior has been born to you today, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be the sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger." If there is a birth through the Virgin and a manifestation in the flesh, how is it not a feeble and empty fable, how is it not madness and nonsense, to ascribe [?] of appearance to so solid and evident [a reality]? For if it was shadow and appearance, and there was neither a true taking of flesh nor a [true] [?] Virgin, then the Word from God the Father did not take hold of the seed of Abraham, being made like [his brothers]. For our condition is in no way mere appearance; we are in bodies that can be touched and seen, clothed in this earth-born flesh, and subject to corruption and passions. Therefore, if the Word did not become flesh, then neither, since he himself suffered when tempted, is he able to help those who are tempted. For he would not suffer anything [?]. So the whole thing truly comes to nothing for us. For what back did he give [to the lash] for us? Or what cheek did he offer to [?], enduring the blows of the Jews? And [how did they fasten] with nails the hands and feet of one who had not appeared in the flesh? In what way could anyone suppose it? Or what side, tell me, did Pilate's soldiers pierce, showing the onlookers the precious blood gushing out together with water? And if we must say something beyond this, Christ neither died for us nor has been raised. If this is accepted as true, faith has been emptied, the cross is gone,

On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten.

— the salvation and life of the world, and the hope of those who have fallen asleep in faith has utterly perished. For blessed Paul too was convinced that this is how things stand: "For I handed on to you as of first importance," he says, "what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles; and last of all, as to one untimely born," he says, "he appeared also to me." And after other things again: "Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then neither has Christ been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty, and our faith is empty too. We are even found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if in fact the dead are not raised." For how, tell me, could a shadow die? How then did the Father raise Christ, if he was shadow and appearance, and could not be caught by the bonds of death? Away, then, with their vomit; let us regard what they say as nothing but the offscourings of an unholy counsel. For the Savior's disciple warns us in advance about such people when he writes: "Many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God." "And this is the [spirit] of the Antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now is already in the world." For if he did not become man, and did not ascend in the flesh to the Father and God in the heavens, neither would he return to us from heaven as man, that is, in the flesh. Or do I not seem to you to speak truly?

B. Very much so.

A. As for others, who out of boundless dullness think and hold that the Word born from God refused birth through the holy Virgin and dishonored our nature, but was rather changed into the flesh from the earth — this is the view of people who blaspheme the dispensation and choose to find fault with the divine counsels. For the Creator of all, the Word of God, rich in mercy, [?] became man for our sake, born of a woman, so that, since the children have shared in blood and flesh, he too might likewise partake of the same, "that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their lives." So said the sacred Scripture. But those who, of so wholly beautiful [Hebrews 2:14–15.]

and excellent a counsel, declare it unbefitting, and, as if they were capable of thinking better, find fault with the counsels of wisdom — they say that we must not ascribe to the Only-begotten birth pangs and delivery from a woman, but should rather suppose that the nature of the Word was transformed into this frail body, and they imagine change in him who knows no change. For the nature of God is firmly founded in its own goods, and has an unshakable permanence in what it is. A created nature, brought into existence in time, might undergo alteration, and that would not lie outside proper and true reasoning. For whatever has received a beginning of being at all has, as it were, the necessity of alteration already sown in it from the start. But God, who is beyond every mind and whose existence is exempt from and transcends generation and corruption, will also be above change. And just as by the principle of his own nature he rises above and surpasses everything called into being, and that by incomparable differences, so too he will rise above what usually befalls the things made through him, not knowing how to suffer [?]. Therefore the divine abides among unchangeable goods, while the things of creation are subject to alteration and change, with corruption at their door. Knowing this very well and reasoning most wisely, the prophet Jeremiah cried out to God: "You sit enthroned forever, and we perish forever." For the divine will always be seated as on its own throne, reigning and ruling over all, and tyrannized by none of the passions. But we, having a nature very easily moved and [?] toward alteration and change, "perish forever" — that is, at every season and time we are corruptible and changeable. So neither could the divine ever come to be subject to change, driven from its own stability by any of the passions, nor could the corruptible and alterable — that is, created — nature be enriched with unchangeability as part of its essence, nor would creation boast of the goods of the divine nature as its own. For it would rightly hear: "What do you have that you did not receive?" That the nature of the Word is wholly unchangeable and unalterable, while created nature is wholly alterable, anyone can see very easily as blessed David sings in the Spirit: "The heavens will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not come to an end." Where, then, has the Word from God remained the same, if it is true to say that, abandoning his firm and unshaken state, he descended into what he was not, [changed] into the nature of flesh and into [subjection to] corruption? How then is it not nonsense, and indeed madness,

B. Certainly.

A. It would then be time, countering their ignorance with something still more ignorant, to say that it is not unreasonable that the flesh from the earth should also at some time [be changed] into the nature of the Godhead

and [enter into] the substance that is highest of all [?]. For if [the Word], as their stupefaction would have it, has passed over into the nature of the flesh, nothing any longer prevents the flesh from soaring above its own lowly nature, and being remolded into Godhead, and [?]. But we will not gratify their senselessness with compliance; rather, we will hold fast to the divine Scriptures. When the prophet says, "Behold, the Virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Emmanuel," and blessed Gabriel seals the prophecy and interprets the decree from above to the Virgin — "Do not be afraid, Mary," he said, "for behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus" — we believe that Emmanuel was truly born of a woman, and, thinking rightly, we will not thrust away the splendid and admirable glory of our own nature.

B. Excellently said. For the Only-begotten took hold not of his own nature (for then our condition would be no better off), nor of that of angels, but of the seed of Abraham, as it is written, so that in this way, and not otherwise, he might rescue the race that had slipped into corruption.

A. And is not this too worthy of wonder, besides what we have said, Hermias?

B. What sort of thing?

A. Some, all but bidding farewell to the divinely inspired Scripture and handing their own minds over to deceiving spirits, have sunk to such folly and childish loathsomeness as to think that the Creator of the ages, the Word coeternal with God the Father, has the beginning of his existence coinciding with the birth of the flesh. They imagine as late-born the one who is beyond every age and time, as though only at the very end, at the time of the incarnation, God became Father, and the one through whom are all things and in whom are all things entered into being and subsistence, as it were, together with the temple from the Virgin. Have they not then driven on to the very height of evils, these people who so readily accepted so old-wivish and loathsome a myth, and filled their own minds with undiluted dullness? "Truly their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they deceive; the venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness."

B. I agree; the Psalmist's word is true.

A. For is it not necessary that he through whom all things exist should exist before all things?

B. Well said.

A. What then would they do, when John writes, "In the beginning was the Word… All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being"? And again: "What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our

eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life — and the life was manifested, and we have seen it, and testify, and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was manifested to us" — and when Christ himself pointed out to the Jews the unsurpassable antiquity of his own existence? For when they said, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" they heard plainly in reply, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am." Since nothing [?] is added to the "was," and the "am" is clearly set down, what beginning of birth could anyone discern? Or how could he who was in the beginning, beyond every mind, admit of being called into existence at some point in time? Now if anyone chose to oppose these people at greater leisure, it would not be hard, by bringing forward the words of the divinely inspired Scripture, to ward off the harm that comes from their stupidity. But things that suffer so obvious a refutation and are so very unseemly are, I think, not even worth troubling about.

B. Well said.

A. Let us go on, then, to what is akin to the view already condemned. For some debase the beauty of the truth, as if counterfeiting a coin, "lifting up their horn on high and speaking injustice against God," as it is written. They imagine the Only-begotten as non-existent and not subsisting as an individual, and not existing in his own hypostasis, but simply a word and a saying, produced by God as mere utterance; and this, the wretches say, dwelt in a man. And having put Jesus together in this way, they say he is holier than the saints, but not God as well. So, as the Savior's disciple wrote: "Who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, the one who denies the Father and the Son. Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; whoever confesses the Son has the Father also." For both are known through both, and each in the other, both by us and by the holy angels. No one could learn what a Father is without conceiving in his mind a Son who subsists and has been begotten; nor again could anyone learn what the Son is unless he wisely considered that the Father has begotten. So I think it necessary and true to say that if the Son does not exist, we could not truly conceive of the Father either. For how can he still be Father, if he has not truly begotten? And if he has begotten what does not subsist or exist at all, what is begotten will be nothing. For what does not subsist is equivalent to nothing, or rather is wholly nothing. Then God will be the Father of nothing. But, my good sirs, I would say to the expounders of such ideas, what you say is idle drivel. Or else tell me, since I ask: how is the love of God the Father toward us exceptional, and [how] did he give for us his

…the Son, who according to you has no subsistence. So then he has given nothing on our behalf; and the Word neither became flesh, nor endured the precious cross, nor abolished the power of death, nor came back to life again. For if, according to you, he is nothing and has no existence, how could he have done any of these things? Then the word of holy Scripture has deceived those who believed, and the firmness of the faith vanishes into nothing.

B. God forbid!

A. What then? Does not the divine word tell us that the Son exists in the form of God, and call him the image and impress of the One who begot him?

B. Certainly.

A. And images are like their archetypes.

B. How could they not be?

A. Then if the image has no subsistence, and the impress is not thought to have an existence of its own, they must grant by necessary reasoning that the one whose impress he is also has no subsistence, and the image's lack of beauty will surely run back to the archetype.

B. Quite so.

A. Then tell me: when Philip, who was very eager to learn, asked to see the Father, saying, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us," did he ask to see the Father who exists and subsists, or one who does not exist and has no subsistence?

B. The one who exists, obviously.

A. If, then, the Son is nothing because he does not subsist, as their unbridled audacity claims, why did he present himself to us as the image and exact knowledge of the Father, saying, "Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? I and the Father are one"? But I do not think anyone could behold the one who subsists in what does not subsist, nor could what exists ever be thought wholly identical with what does not exist. How will the Father be in the Son, and the Son in turn in the Father? Or is it not true to say that if the Word does not exist with an existence of his own, the Father himself would be in danger, since he would have nothing within himself and would be thought to exist in nothing? For what does not exist at all could no longer be thought of as anything.

B. The argument is not harsh [?]. For our opponents' doctrine suffers from the greatest absurdity in itself, and yet the argument brings it round to discord.

A. One might reasonably wonder how the Father made the things that exist in a Son who has no being. And if someone were to ask which is better [?] for existing things, the Son [?] of the Father, from whose [essence] he shone forth without beginning, he who expresses the pure essence [?] (he destroys his own part [?]). That is:

is it good to be, or not to be [?]? How would you answer?

B. I would say that being is good. For the creator, who gives being to things that once were not, is good in the highest degree [?], and he is the creator.

A. Excellently said, for that is the nature of the matter. Then creation is in a better state, if the one through whom all things are called into being is said not to subsist, while they have been brought forth [?] and are understood to be in being.

B. Away with such blasphemy! For "the Word of God is living and active," as it is written. That is why he also said, "I am the life."

A. But what does not subsist [?] could not be thought of as life. Yet he is life by nature, for he [dies?] in no way [?]. So the claim that the Word who appeared from God does not subsist is a rotten falsehood and the scum [?] of a most foolish mind.

B. Entirely. For he himself said to Moses, "I am He Who Is." And how could what truly is be thought to [exist?] if it is not preserved in a subsistence of its own?

A. Then we rightly perceive the utter ignorance of those who have held such views.

B. Quite so.

A. Nor, Hermias, would we praise those either, we who have been thoroughly taught to be keen hunters of the truth.

A. I mean those who say that flesh [without a soul?] was united to the Word. For they clothe the Word with flesh alone, which has only a living and sensitive motion, and bring him into the world in that way, assigning the activity of mind and soul to the Only-begotten. For they shudder, I do not know how to put it, at confessing that the Word was united to a man complete according to the definition of humanity, that is, one made of soul and body. They count the tradition of the faith, which comes from above and is most ancient, as of no account at all, and have ignorantly chosen to follow only their own will and human reasonings, not truly thinking as they ought [?].

B. And what is their argument for this [?]?

A. I will tell you. We say that the Mediator [?] between God and men, according to the Scriptures, is composed of a humanity that is complete according to its own definition, as we hold [?], and of the Son who appeared from God by nature, that is, the Only-begotten. We affirm that an ineffable concurrence into union, beyond reason, has been effected between unequal and unlike natures. Yet we acknowledge one Christ and Lord and Son, who is and is understood as God and man at once. And we are accustomed to keep the union entirely undivided, believing that the same one is both [Only-begotten and Firstborn?]: Only-begotten as the Word from God the Father, who shone forth from his essence; Firstborn since he became man, and that among many brothers.

For just as there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, so also there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. [?] … the Word through whom are all things, [who] became flesh, that is, man.

A. But their views do not entirely agree with what we hold on this matter. For they too admittedly accept one Christ Jesus, and in this at least they think excellently. They also emphatically refuse, as the height of impiety, to divide the Emmanuel into two. Yet they strip the flesh of the human and rational soul, and say that it was united to the Word of God [?]. And they have, as they think, a persuasive argument for this. For things that have come together by composition to form one complete whole, they say, [are each incomplete?], not being complete by themselves and in a nature of their own, but needing composition from parts. Therefore, they say, we must not grant [?] that the temple united to the Word is complete, so that the composition, whatever it is that is perceived in Christ, may keep its own definition precise and beyond reproach. And they might add this too, I suppose: if, they say, we compose the Emmanuel out of a complete man and the Word who is from the Father, the danger is not small, or rather it is inescapable. For how will it not then appear that we must, even against our will,

B. Then what shall we say in reply to this?

A. First, that the tradition of the faith, which is so very ancient and has come down to us from the holy apostles themselves, should not be whittled away [?] by excessive precision; nor should things beyond the mind be subjected to exhaustive inquiries. Nor should we step forward like those who rashly declare that one thing was done rightly, while another ought to have been otherwise and would truly have been better. Rather we should leave to the all-wise God the course of his own counsels, and not arrogantly find fault with what he has judged to be good. For we shall hear him saying plainly, "For my counsels are not like your counsels, nor are my ways like your ways; but as far as heaven is from the earth, so far is my way from your ways, and your thoughts from my mind." Next, what they think they have cleverly discovered will be shown to be utterly stale and ignorant. For if someone chose to strip that divine temple of its rational soul, the union will not be of two incomplete things [?] … [?]. For admittedly, in relation to the whole man, I mean the man made of soul and body, the flesh alone and by

itself is a part. But God would not be called [a part?] … [?] … nor will the concurrence be [?] of incomplete things, if it is of the complete Word and of flesh that is incomplete as far as the definition of a complete man, whole in his own nature, is concerned [?]. We shall not worship two, nor shall we speak of two Christs, even if we say that the concurrence into the unity of the Emmanuel was effected from a complete man and from the Word of God. According to what seems right to them, even if he is said to be made of the flesh alone and the Word who appeared from God the Father, no argument will persuade them to confess a pair of Christs, though they posit the flesh as a part and the Only-begotten in turn as a part [?]. Instead they accept the Emmanuel as one Lord Jesus Christ, and in this they seem to think very rightly. In just the same way, even if we say that the Word from God was, as it were, brought together and united ineffably and beyond understanding with a complete man (that is, clearly, one made of soul and body), we shall not conceive of a pair of sons. We shall conceive of one and the same, who is God by nature and has shone forth from the very essence of the Father, and who in the last times of the age became man, and [was born] of the holy Virgin,

and is worshiped by us [and by the holy] angels, according to the Scriptures.

B. What then if they say that our nature [?] had no need of the Only-begotten's coming among us, but that, wishing to be seen by those on earth, to live among men, and to show us the way of the life of the Gospel, he put on, by the economy, flesh like ours? For the divine, by its own nature, [is] not

A. They will be shown to have no idea of the purpose of the incarnation, and not to have grasped at all the great mystery of godliness. For suppose the incarnation, or becoming man, of the Only-begotten had as its only occasion that he should be seen by those on earth, and conferred [?] nothing else on human nature. How then would it not already be better and wiser for us too to agree with the opinion of the Docetists? Those wretches clothe the Word with neither flesh nor an earthly body, and invent the myth that he was seen as a man; yet they have plainly acknowledged that he became the bringer of the finest things. Or will you not say that, if the Word from God does human nature no good at all and did not become flesh, it is better that he be free of the encumbrance [?] of the flesh, and merely seem to have made use of an earthly body once, and so accomplish the purpose set before him?

B. What then would be the reason for his coming among us, or what is the manner of his becoming man, and for what purpose was it done? I should like to learn.

A. Come, then, my noble friend: [take hold?] of the sacred Scriptures, fix the eye of your mind firmly on the words of the holy apostles, and look

at what we are seeking. Now the divine Paul, who had Christ speaking within him, said to us: "Since the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives." And elsewhere, explaining to us another aspect, he says: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." Is it not, then, perfectly evident, and unclear to none of the [wise?], that the Only-begotten became as we are, that is, a complete man? He did so in order to free our earthly body from the corruption that had been brought in upon it, having come down by the economy of the union into identity [?] according to the law of life. And by making the human soul his own, he would render it superior to sin, dyeing it, as with a dye, with the firmness and unchangeableness of his own nature.

B. I do not think the matter is unclear. For it carries within itself the reasonable account, or rather the true one.

A. Since the flesh became the flesh of the Word who gives life to all things, it rises above the power of death and corruption. In the same way, I think, since the soul became the soul of one who does not know how to sin, it now has a steadfast and unalterable stability in all good things, incomparably stronger than the sin that once tyrannized over it. For Christ is the first man who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. He has been set as the root and firstfruits of those who are being refashioned in the Spirit for newness of life, so that he might pass on to the whole human race, by participation and grace, both the incorruption of the body and the security and firmness of the divinity. Knowing this, the divine Paul writes: "For as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one." By the image of the man of dust he meant our proneness to slip into sin, and the death that was thrown upon us as a result; and by the image of the heavenly one, that is, Christ, he meant steadfastness in sanctification, and our recovery and renewal from death and corruption to incorruption and life. We say, then, that the Word was united whole with a whole man. For he would surely not have treated the better part of us, the soul, as of no account, and granted the labors of his coming among us to the flesh alone. The mystery of the economy was well accomplished through both. As an instrument, he made use of his own flesh for the works of the flesh and its natural weaknesses, as many as are far from blame; and of his own soul in turn for the human and blameless passions. [Isa. 53:9; 1 Pet. 2:22]

For he is said to have [?] borne the fatigue of long journeys, alarm and fear, grief and agony, and death on the cross. With no one compelling him, he laid down his own soul for us of his own accord, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. He paid his own flesh in exchange for the flesh of all, a truly equivalent gift, and made his soul a ransom for the soul of all, even though he came back to life again, since as God he is life by nature. And indeed the divine Peter says: "Brothers, I may speak to you freely about the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to set one of the fruit of his loins upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." For it is not right to say that the flesh united to the Word could be held by perpetual corruption, or that the divine soul could be held fast by the gates of Hades. For it was not abandoned to Hades, as the divine Peter said. He is surely not saying that the nature which is wholly beyond the grasp and reach of death, that is, the divinity of the Only-begotten, was brought back up from the depths beneath the earth. That would not have been thought anything to marvel at, if the Word from God did not remain in Hades, since by the activity and nature of his divinity he wondrously and beyond reason fills all things and is present to all. For the divine is above place, limitation and measurable magnitude, and is itself contained by nothing. What is wondrous, and what all beings marvel at, is that the body, which is corruptible by nature, came back to life, for it had been united to the incorruptible Word. And the divine soul, which had been brought together with him and united to him, went down into Hades, but using a power and authority befitting God, it appeared to the spirits there as well. That is why he said to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Be uncovered." And it seems to me that the blessed Peter also said something of this kind about the Word of God and his soul, which had become his by the economy of the union: "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if the will of God should so will, than for doing evil. For Christ also died once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit; in which," he says, "he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who once had been disobedient." For I do not think they would say that the divinity of the Only-begotten, bare and by itself, went down into Hades and preached to the spirits there while remaining entirely invisible. For the divine is always beyond being seen. Nor shall we grant that it was shaped into the form of a soul in mere seeming and as a semblance, for seeming must be rejected everywhere. Rather, just as he preached to those still in the flesh, so also to the souls in Hades

he preached, having as his own vehicle the soul united to him. The manner of the union is perhaps deep and truly ineffable, and beyond the grasp of our minds. Yet we ought to consider this: to meddle in things beyond us is not without harm, and it is utterly senseless to put what is beyond the mind to the rack and to try to understand what cannot be understood. Or do you not know that this deep mystery, which surpasses the mind within us, is honored by a faith that does not pry? Leaving to Nicodemus and those like him the foolish question [?], "How can these things be?", we shall accept without hesitation what is declared as an oracle through the divine Spirit, and believe Christ himself when he says, "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen."

B. Well said.

A. Away, then, with all nonsense, feeble myth, false opinion and the deceit of elaborate words! For we do not admit what is by nature harmful, even if our opponents should beat us down with highly polished, and even bitter, words. For our divine mystery does not rest on persuasive words of human wisdom, but on

[What God] did not wish us to know, let us not force ourselves to learn; nor shall we know it (for how could we, if God does not wish it?). And that inquiring brings danger upon us [?] … [?] teaches that it happens in the way he himself knows [?] … [of the soul?], unless some power from God is given to the speaker and grace blossoms on what is said; and this too does not come about without God for those who [?] effectively. He says, at any rate, in the sixty-seventh Psalm: "For he will give a word to those who preach the gospel with great power." [?]

demonstration of the Spirit. Being, then, God and Lord of all according to the Scriptures, the Only-begotten appeared to us. For he was seen on earth, and shone upon those in darkness, having become man. He did not do so in mere seeming, God forbid, for it is madness to think or say that. Nor was he changed into flesh by transformation and alteration, for the Word from God is unalterable, and is always the same and remains in the same state. Nor does his existence begin at the same time as the flesh, for he is the maker of the ages. Nor did he come to be in a man as a word without subsistence or as a bare utterance, for he who calls things that once were not into existence and being must necessarily exist before them; he is the one who is life by nature, from the life of God and [the Father?], existing and understood in his own hypostasis. Nor did he put on flesh alone, bereft of a rational soul. Rather, he was truly born of a woman, and the living and subsisting God the Word, coeternal with God the Father, appeared as man, taking the form of a servant. And just as he is complete in divinity, so he is also complete in humanity. He is not composed of divinity alone and flesh into one Christ and Lord and Son, but of two complete things, I mean humanity and divinity, wondrously [united] into one and the same.

B. Whom, then, did the holy Virgin bear? The man, or the Word from God?

[Instead of "in persuasive words of wisdom," he reads "in persuasive [words] of human [wisdom]." [?] "Stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it" [?] which all [?] …]

…to miss what is fitting and true. Do not divide him for me. Do not separate him into a man on one side and God the Word on the other, and so present us with a two-faced Emmanuel. Otherwise someone might rightly reproach us for choosing to think nothing correct, and preferring instead the very things that holy Scripture has condemned. For one of Christ's disciples said this: “But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They told you that in the last times there will be scoffers, scoffing and following their own ungodly desires. These are the ones who cause divisions; they are worldly and do not have the Spirit.”

B. So must we make no distinction of any kind?

A. Certainly not, at least to the point of speaking of two after the union and thinking of each one separately. Still, it should be understood that the mind does perceive a certain difference between the natures, for divinity and humanity are by no means the same thing. Yet along with its thoughts about these, the mind will also accept that the two have come together into unity. So he is from God the Father as God, and from the Virgin as man. The Word who shone forth from God the Father, ineffably and beyond understanding, is said to have been born through a woman as well. He came down into humanity and lowered himself into what he was not. He did this not in order to remain emptied, but so that he might be believed to be God even when he appeared on earth in a form like ours. He did not dwell in a man; he himself became man by nature, while also recovering his own glory.

The divine Paul gathers into one, by the economy, divinity and humanity: things that stand far apart in substance and are separated by an immeasurable difference. From both he points to the one Christ, who is both Son and God, when he says: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and who was designated Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness.” Look: he clearly says that he himself was set apart for the gospel of God. Yet he openly writes, “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord,” and again, “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Having named him Son of God, he says that he was born of the seed of David, and he insists that he was designated, and designated as Son of God at that. Tell me, then: how is the one who sprang from the seed of David God? And how was the one who is Son before the ages and eternally, inasmuch as he came forth from God, designated Son of God, as though he were being brought to the beginning of his existence? For he said of himself: “The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” And yet the word [?“today”] always signifies to us not the past but rather the present, and…

B. I am more than a little perplexed. But I would say yes [?]… being saved [?] by the Father… and shall we then strip Emmanuel of being life by nature? Or shall we do what deserves praise: refer to his humanity and to the measure of our nature whatever is lowly in his words, and from the things that show him to be God behold his glory that is above the world, understanding that the same one is both man and God, or rather God made man?

B. Explain how.

A. Let the most esteemed Paul come forward, then, crying out and saying: “We speak wisdom among the mature, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away…

…hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and which none of the rulers of this age understood. For if they had understood it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” In addition to this: “He is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance, and he upholds all things by the word of his power. Having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.” Now, to be the Lord of glory and to be called by that name: how is this not exceedingly exalted and beyond everything that has come into being and been brought into existence? I pass over human things, for they are very small. But I will say this: even if someone named the Angels, and listed Principalities and Thrones and Dominions, and even mentioned the highest Seraphim, he would admit that they all fall short of such exalted glory, so long as his mind is not corrupted. For I say that this honour is unique and must be reserved for the nature that is sovereign over all things, and for it alone. How then could the one who was crucified be the Lord of glory? And the radiance of the Father, the imprint of his being, who upholds all things by the word of his power, is said to have become superior to the angels. I suppose this is because he took the lesser place when he appeared as man. For it is written: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death.” Shall we then strip the Word who came forth from God the Father of the pre-eminence of being that belongs to him and of his exact likeness to the Father, because we see him outranked by the glory of the angels on account of the lowliness of the economy?

B. Certainly not. I think we must neither entirely remove the Word from God from human things after his union with flesh, nor deprive the human of the glory that befits God, if it is conceived and spoken of in Christ. But you should know that some people ask: “Who, then, is truly Jesus the Christ? The man born of a woman, or the Word from God?”

A. It is utterly foolish to strain over pointless questions and to answer back with idle chatter. Still, I will say that it is dangerous and harmful to cut him in two and set man and Word apart. The economy does not allow it, and the divinely inspired Scripture proclaims one Christ. For my part, I say that neither the Word from God apart from humanity, nor the temple born of a woman without being united to the Word, should be called Christ Jesus. The Word from God, brought together ineffably with humanity in a union according to the economy, is understood to be Christ. As God and Son by nature he is higher than humanity; as man he is somewhat beneath the glory that befits God. That is why at one time he said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. I and the Father are one,” and at another time, “My Father is greater than I.”

He is not less than the Father as regards identity of substance, or in any respect of equality whatever. Yet he says that he is in a lesser position because of his humanity. The sacred Scriptures also proclaim him sometimes as wholly man, with his divinity passed over in silence for the sake of the economy, and sometimes as God, with his humanity left unmentioned. But he is in no way wronged by this, because the two have come together into unity.

B. What do you mean? I don't quite understand.

A. The Hebrew of Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin, the called apostle, writes to those who have been justified through faith and have put to death the members of the flesh, by which I mean fornication, passion, evil desire and greed: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” And Christ himself said about his disciples: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, those you have given me, and I guarded them, and not one of them was lost except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I am coming to you, and I say these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.” Do you see, then, how in these passages he seems to us to be described from the standpoint of his humanity alone?

B. You are quite right.

A. Yet we will surely not suppose that he is hidden and absent from the world, since he clearly says: “Truly, truly, I say to you, where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them.” And again: “Look, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” And you can see the most holy Paul himself often not bothering to proclaim that he is also man. He says: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ.” And again: “I make known to you,” he says, “the gospel that was preached by me, that it is not of human origin. For I did not receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere he says: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we no longer know him in that way.” Who, then, is Jesus the Christ, who flashes into him so ineffable, unerring and divine a revelation of his own mysteries? Is it not the Word who became flesh, and who for our sake did not disdain to be born of a woman?

B. Certainly. I remember blessed Gabriel saying to the holy Virgin: “Do not be afraid, Mary; for you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.” [?]

And I think this new name was given to the Word by the Father through the angel's voice. A prophetic oracle had already cried out beforehand: “And they will call him by his new name, which the Lord will give him.”

A. When the one who is coeternal with the Father, the Son and Only-begotten before every age, became man in the last times of the age, he was born through a woman, was designated son, was also called firstborn, and came to be among many brothers. At that point the Father by nature also bestows the name, following the laws of fatherhood, so to speak. You would delight us too, having understood the manner of the economy so well.

B. So the same one is both only-begotten and firstborn.

A. My friend, do not suppose that it is any other way. The Only-begotten as God is firstborn among us by the union of the economy, and he is among many brothers as man. This is so that we too may be sons of God in him and through him, both by nature and by grace: by nature as it is in him, and in him alone; by participation and by grace as it is in us, through him, in the Spirit. Being the Only-begotten became proper to the humanity in Christ, because it is united to the Word through the coming-together of the economy. In the same way, being among many brothers and being firstborn became proper to the Word, because he is united to flesh. But he holds firmly to his being God and is always beyond change, so he does not depart from his own glory. That is why the holy and blessed multitude of the spirits above has been commanded, along with us, to worship him. It would surely have been quite likely that they would refuse to worship him and hesitate to honour him when they saw the lowliness of his humanity. They might not have thought it right to give glory to the one who for our sake became like us, keeping as far as possible from any appearance of going astray. For even to them the mystery of Christ was still unseen. But the Spirit revealed it to them, and did not allow the sanctified ones to fall into impiety. That is why the divine Paul says: “And when he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: And let all [?] … God names [?], because he is by nature, and through this shows [?] … for to a man perhaps properly [?], it would be nothing to God. But from the things by which he is [?] … he is named [?]: Light, and [?], and Power, and Truth, Only-begotten, and Radiance, and Imprint of the one who begot him, Mercy, and Wisdom, and Righteousness [?] … trespasses. Having become man I shall be called Jesus, which means Saviour; for I shall carry out that economy for the salvation of sinners.

…the angels of God worship him.” For the one who by the property of his nature is distinct from the whole inhabited world, and as God is outside it, entered into it and appeared as part of the world as man. But he did not on that account slip from the divine glory. He is worshipped as only-begotten even if he is called firstborn, and that title clearly suits the measures of humanity above all.

B. Shall we then worship Emmanuel as a man?

A. Heaven forbid! That is nonsense, deception and error. We would be no different from those who have worshipped the creation rather than the Creator and Maker, who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, as it is written. If we think like them, we will certainly hear the same charge with them: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed animals and reptiles.” Shall we not ourselves be acting and thinking just like those people, exchanging the glory of God for a lie, for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, if we offer worship as to a mere man, one of our own kind, to the…

B. Very much so.

A. What then? Did not even the host of angels above [?] those who have come to this pitch of madness [?]?

A. I think we shall also fasten an inescapable charge of error on the herd of the Gentiles, and the harm done by their ancient offences will be hard to wash away. For I think they are in error even now, no less than of old, and have not known the path that leads straight ahead. And it seems the blessed Paul is wasting his words when he addresses them and says: “Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to beings that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements? Do you want to be enslaved to them all over again?” What God have they come to know at all, if Christ, in whom they have believed, is not God by nature? And if they have worshipped a man, they are caught in the snares of the ancient error. Or is what I say not true?

B. It certainly is.

A. See, then, how necessary reasoning practically forces us, even against our will, to conclude that we must wisely worship the Son as God by nature, even when he has appeared in a form like ours. Their coming together into unity is fully able to remove whatever at times causes distress by raising the suspicion of mere humanity.
A. For when the nature of the Word took on what is human, it did not become mere humanity. Rather, it prevails over what it assumed by its own glory, and is preserved in an unshaken continuance…

…of the glory that befits God. The disciples thought this when they worshipped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God,” even though they saw him walking along, in flesh like ours. For he was miraculously running along the crest of the waves.

B. And who was it that said to the woman in Samaria, “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know”? How then can the one who is ranked among the worshippers be worshipped?

A. My friend, you keep crying out this little word “who”, invented somehow by people without understanding. Christ is in no way divided. The one speaking to the woman was the one and only Lord Jesus Christ, ineffably composed of the humanity that worships and the divinity that is worshipped. One might also put it another way. Insofar as he is God, he would be understood to be himself the Lord of glory. But insofar as he became man, glorified by sharing in the glory that comes from God, he also needed glory, and said, “Father, glorify your Son.” Yet there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism,” as it is written. There is one faith, faith in Christ, and truly one baptism, even though we are baptized into and believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the same way and for the same reason, I think, there is one worship of the Father, of the Son who became man, and of the Holy Spirit. The Only-begotten will in no way be excluded from being worshipped by us and by the holy angels, even if he became flesh and dwelt among us, and was called firstborn among many brothers. Otherwise, what would remain of the principle of faith in him? How is it not right to [?]… For I think that those who choose to think rightly would not say that we have believed in the Word born of God alone, stripping him of the flesh. Nor shall we omit to say the following, for it must be said.

B. What do you mean?

A. Faith is not directed toward one of us, or toward a man, but toward the one who is God by nature and truly, in the person of Christ. The wise Paul will support this argument when he writes: “For we did not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Christ's sake. For God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ.” See how clearly and plainly the light of the knowledge of God the Father shone forth in the face of Christ. That is why he also said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father; I and the Father are one.” The divine imprint is not bodily. It consists in power and in glory most fitting to God, and this was present in Christ in its purity. He wished to be known through these things as well. Through the excellence of his deeds he wanted his hearers to rise up to the right thoughts about him, while the visible flesh quietly made him seem small. “For if I do not do…

…placing your faith in one who is in the flesh, you will not have believed simply in a man, but in the Father himself, through me. I am the Son, equal to him in every respect and without any variation. I became flesh for your sake and made my own the lowly covering, the humanity. Yet I have [?] and equal power of action, and remain wholly inseparable from him in identity of glory, toward…

A. You can also learn in another way that he does not reject faith, but receives it as directed to his own person, without any division or distinction, even though he became flesh. When he healed the man blind from birth and gave him the sweet, though unfamiliar, gift of light, everyone was rightly amazed at him. The man freed from his affliction was put on trial by the Jews, and he acknowledged his healer. Then Christ met him and said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” The man cried out, “Who is he, Lord, so that I may believe in him?” And he answered, “You have seen him, and he is the one speaking with you.” The man said, “I believe, Lord.” And he worshipped him. Yet surely it is obvious to everyone that the divine and supreme nature is entirely invisible. “For no one has ever seen God,” as it is written. Suppose, then, that the Word from God the Father had separated the human from himself, as though he had merely appeared in that form, and wished to be believed in bare and alone. Why, then, did he not instead tell the man he had helped to reflect on the nature of God, whatever it may be? Instead he pointed to himself bodily, as someone present for them to see with their own eyes. For he said, “You have seen him, and he is the one speaking with you.” Shall we not say that he pointed to the flesh?

B. Certainly.

A. How, then, could the flesh be himself, unless it is understood that by the union he himself is what is his own, just as would indeed be the case with us? For one could point to a man like us, not in a divided or incomplete way: I mean the one composed of soul…

…and of body, and from his flesh alone.
B. I agree; you are right.
A. Our wise John has written somewhere: “Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” And one would be no less amazed at the divine Peter, who addressed the Jews clearly and openly: “Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a sick man, and how this man has been healed, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man stands before you in good health.” And again, a little later: “There is salvation in no one else; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” Who, then, both underwent death and was raised in glory, and is from Nazareth, if not Jesus Christ? That is, the one ineffably begotten of the Father before every age, but who in the last time, as the age was coming to its end, was also born bodily of a woman. So whoever accepts faith in him will carry off the choicest prize, for he will be called a son of God. “For to all who received him,” it says, “he gave authority to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” For he was born through a woman so that he himself might have first place in all things, as it is written. But since he is the firstfruits of the creation that is being refashioned toward God through sanctification, he was shown, before all others, to be born of the Spirit. He passed over the union of man and woman. He did not condemn nature to dishonor and blame, for marriage is honorable, and he who fashioned them in the beginning made them male and female. Rather, he was in some way already assigning human things to what is greater and incomparably superior. For he wished us no longer to be called the offspring of men, but of the Spirit. And indeed he says: “Call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, the heavenly one, and you are all brothers.” Believing in him, then, is altogether blameless; more than that, it is honored with the forgetting of offenses. For the eminent Paul writes again: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus.” I will not hesitate at all to come back and repeat what I have already said: Christ Jesus is not understood as the Word from God bare and by himself. Rather, when he took on the hu- [1 Cor. 15 [?]; Gen. 1 [?]]

-man, he was joined to flesh. It was as he was in this state, visible and in a form like ours, that the Father showed him to the holy apostles, sending forth from above a voice like this: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” Notice, then, that he does not say, “My Son is in this one.” This was so that he would not be thought of as divided, as though one were in another, but understood as one and the same by the union of the economy. John will convince us that to contradict this is an offense, and one of the most dangerous. For he writes that this is the testimony of God, the testimony he has given concerning his Son: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son.” And God has testified that “This one, who is with flesh and in the form of a servant, is uniquely and properly, truly, my Son.” What then? Shall we not grant that the glorious grace of holy baptism, the life given in it, and our participation in God through sanctification in the Spirit have been accomplished through Jesus Christ?
B. We must. For I remember John saying: “He who comes after me is mightier than I; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and

A. Then shall we say, my friend, that being able to baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire is the work of a humanity like ours?
B. How could that be?
A. And yet John called him a man, the one who was about to appear and be seen, and said that he baptizes with fire and the Holy Spirit. He does not infuse into the baptized a Spirit foreign to himself, in the manner of a servant or assistant. He does it as God by nature, with supreme authority, giving the Spirit that is from him and his own, through whom the divine stamp is impressed on us. For we are refashioned as into the divine image, into Christ Jesus. This is not by undergoing a bodily remolding (it would be utterly foolish to think that). It is by partaking of the Holy Spirit and being rich with Christ himself within us, so that we now cry out joyfully: “Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness.” “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ,” it says.
B. Have we, then, been baptized into a man, and shall we say that this is true?
A. Hush, man! What are you doing, sir? You are dragging our hope down to earth. We have been baptized not into a mere man, but into God made man, who releases from punishment and from the ancient charges those who have received faith in him. And indeed the divine Peter, addressing the Jews, said: “Repent, then, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness

of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” For when he has released from sin the one who has given himself to him, he then anoints him with his own Spirit. As the Word from God the Father, he himself sends this Spirit forth and makes it spring up for us from his own nature. But because of the union he also makes the matter common, as it were, to the economy in the flesh, and so as a man he breathed the Spirit bodily. For he breathed on the apostles, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” And he does not give the Spirit by measure, as John says; he himself sends it forth from himself, just as the Father certainly does. Indeed the divine Paul, setting aside any difference here, can be seen sometimes attributing the Spirit to God the Father himself and sometimes to the Son. For he writes: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.”
B. It is settled, then, that the Spirit is the Son’s own, and not only insofar as he is the Word who came forth from the Father, but also insofar as he is understood to have become a man like us…

A. The Spirit is his own as he is from the Father, in the consubstantial offspring, the Word who sprang from him. This is so even if he is said to have received the Spirit when he became man, though he possesses the properties of the Godhead as in his own nature. Indeed, though he himself is the life of all things because of his ineffable generation from the living Father, he is said to be made alive along with us. Still, one can see him granting to his own flesh the glory of the activity that befits God, and in turn making the things of the flesh his own and, as it were, attaching them to his own nature by the union of the economy.
B. In what way do you mean?
A. Will you not say that it belongs above all to the Word, who is truly and by nature from God the Father, to come from above and from heaven, and to be able to give life to whomever he wishes to give it?

A. What then? Tell me, would you grant that creating, as God creates, is a human thing?
B. I would not.
A. Why, then, does he give us life as God, and not only through participation in the Holy Spirit, but also by setting before us as food the flesh he assumed? For he said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.” Once the Jews mocked him and somehow tried to award the prize for the better gifts to blessed Moses, saying openly: “Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’ What sign do you do, so that we may believe you? What work do you do, as though bringing the bread [?] down to us from above, from heaven?” To this he says:

“Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” And besides this, he again all but points to himself with his finger as one with a body, saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.” And yet how would it not be accurate to say that the flesh did not come down from heaven, but was from the Virgin, according to the Scriptures? But in countless sayings we can see the Word not dividing himself, but gathering both into one and, as it were, blending the properties of the natures with each other. Nicodemus did not understand the mystery and cried out in ignorance, “How can these things be?” To him he says: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son [?] of God.” And again to the Jews, who suffered from the same ignorance as Nicodemus and somehow chose to laugh at him, he said [?] that his own body too was from heaven: “Does this offend you? Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” Or shall we not say that Emmanuel was born of a woman?
B. How could we not?
A. Where, then, was he before? Or how did he ascend to where he himself says he was, even though the body united to him was born through the holy Virgin? And would we not also confess that flesh from the earth, as far as its own nature goes, can do nothing toward giving life?

A. Then tell me, how is the flesh life-giving? Or how could what is from the earth be understood as also from heaven?
B. By its union, I think, with the Word who is living and from heaven.
A. Be assured that you have reasoned very rightly and in agreement with the sacred words. It could be no other way. And he is Creator, as God is, even when he is not understood apart from the flesh.

…and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might come to have first place in all things. For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in the heavens.” See, again he says openly that all things were created through him and for him. He also says that he is before all things and that all things hold together in him, and that he is the firstborn from the dead, who made peace through his blood for things in the heavens and things on earth. Who, then, is the firstborn from the dead, if not Christ Jesus, that is, the Word in flesh and with flesh? For the Word, being God, would surely not have died. Nor would he be understood as Creator of all things while being a man like us, unless he created as God, and unless after the union he is not understood apart from flesh. He is firstborn from the dead insofar as he appeared as man, without ceasing to be God because of the incarnation. Do you think anyone should find fault with this?
B. Not in the least.
A. You may also see the Spirit-bearers elsewhere taking the same line. John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.” And Paul in turn says: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things; one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” But suppose that, after the Word was united to flesh, something came between them and split him into two different beings—I mean the pair of sons, as it were, that you have in mind. How, then, would all things have been created through Jesus Christ? Yet all things were in fact created through him. It is plain, then, that what belongs naturally and properly to the only Word from the Father was kept for him even when he became flesh. So it is dangerous to dare to divide him. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and through him the Father created all things.

A. He is, then, both Creator, as God, and life-giver, as life. Yet he is also human, and with properties beyond the human, combined into one thing that stands between. For he is the mediator between God and men, according to the Scriptures. He is God by nature, and not without flesh. He is truly man, and not a mere man like us, but remaining what he was even though he became flesh. For it is written: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Do we not believe that Emmanuel was born through the holy Virgin

in the last times of the age?
B. Yes. We will not contradict the divine Scriptures.
A. Then tell me, my friend, would not “yesterday” and “today” signify for us the present time and the time already past?

A. How, then, could he be the same in the past, when he had not yet received birth according to the flesh?
B. Because the Word also was in the beginning. Since he came forth from God the Father, who is eternal and unchangeable, he too has eternity and unchangeability as in his own nature.
A. I commend this view; it is so, and very rightly said. But still, for one who is eager to learn, would you explain, my

A. Is not “Jesus Christ” a very recent name for the Word, one that came with the times of the incarnation?
B. And indeed this, for us, through very many

A. Understand, then, that he says it is Christ Jesus, and not the Word alone, who is the same yesterday and today and forever. But how could human nature have unchangeability and remain always the same, when it undergoes change, first of all the change from non-being to being and living?
B. So the sacred Scripture has missed the truth, saying that the one who did not exist yesterday existed before?
A. I would not say that. Far from it. Christ Jesus is the same yesterday and today and forever. I will by no means deny that the Word is supremely ancient and unchanging, even though he became flesh. But I will hold that, by his union with his own flesh, he is shown in turn to have existed yesterday and before. And indeed the senseless Jew loathed this and tried to stone him, not accepting the faith. For he was astonished that, though seen as a man like us, he testified that he himself was older, with an antiquity beyond any man’s, saying as God: “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am.” To this they replied: “You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?” John too said: “He who comes after me has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me.” And yet, knowing Emmanuel as a man and calling him one, how does he say that one who was born later and after him came to be ahead of him and before him?
B. He says that he came to be ahead of him and before him in glory. That is how it occurs to me to understand it.
A. Yet you will learn, without long arguments, that this interpretation is false and ignorant. For if we accept

“ahead” as meaning superiority in glory, then by the same reasoning we shall say that “after” plainly means second in renown.
B. Then it would follow, it seems, that Christ is inferior to John in glory, and one would foolishly suppose that he ran behind him. For John said, “After me comes a man.”
A. What an absurdity! We will not think it is so, since we have rightly understood what is written in the Psalms: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? And who among the sons of God shall be like God?” So we must attribute supreme antiquity to him even with the flesh, as to one who is God by nature united to flesh, and who is accustomed to share the goods of his own nature with his own

B. Excellently said.
A. You may learn from other testimonies too, my good sir, if you wish, that this is so and is rightly said. For somewhere God spoke through one of the holy prophets about the one from the seed of David, that is, Christ according to the flesh: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are too small to be among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” And the most holy Paul says concerning the sons of Israel: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” See, then, in Christ Jesus, by the union of the economy, the supreme antiquity that properly belongs to the Word. Or is the statement not clear? For he says plainly that the Bethlehemite, as man and born of a woman, has his goings forth from eternity [?]. For the Word who became man was in the beginning and before every age. He himself was the rock, flooding thirsty Israel with unhoped-for and unexpected streams, even though he was born according to the flesh and as man in the last times, and anointed by God the Father for his mission to the world. For it was for no other reason than this that he was named Christ, and the rock was Christ, according to Paul. Or will you say the matter is doubtful?

A. The wise John will also approve this argument and fight alongside it. He all but gathers the natures together and brings the force of the properties fitting to each into a meeting point. See what he says: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—the life was revealed, and we have seen it and testify to it, and we declare to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us.” See, he says clearly that the one who was from the beginning submitted to being seen and touched. For Thomas cried out, “My Lord and my God!” after measuring with his finger the si-

-de of the body and the holes made by the nails. And our divine Luke also says that the holy apostles became eyewitnesses and servants of the Word. For the bodiless one became visible, and the untouchable became touchable. He no longer had the flesh from the earth as a foreign covering, but had made it his own temple, and was known together with it as God and Lord. And you surely know that the most holy Paul wrote: “For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. For this is why Christ died and lived, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.” It is settled, then, that he has truly become Lord of the dead and the living, who died and was raised for this reason alone and no other…

A. Whom, then, my noble friend, do we say underwent death and came back to life?
B. The Son, clearly.
A. You are right that it was the Son, and I commend you. But I would like to learn from you whether the Word from God the Father is mortal and subject to corruption, or is above death and corruption, being superior to them as life.
B. I say the latter.
A. Then how did he come to be among the dead, though he was free, according to the Scriptures? For surely the Word would not have died by himself.
B. Because his flesh died, he himself is said to have suffered this.
A. Most correctly and without error. So it was not apart from the flesh, but rather together with it and with it, that he who died and rose according to the law [?] and nature that are ours crowned himself with the glory of lordship. He showed that dying is a human experience, but coming back to life a divine work, so that through both he might be known as at once like us and above us, as God of all things, and, having come to be with us, might be seen with the Father. So Nathanael, recognizing him, said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel.” And he himself says to his disciples: “You call me Lord and Teacher, and you are right, for that is what I am.” [?] Believed in, he forgives sins, and he gave authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness among the people. Was it not in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth that the man lame in both feet, who sat at the Beautiful Gate, was healed? And Aeneas shook off a long illness and escaped a disease very hard to be rid of. The divine Paul said to him: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you.”

[?] …and earnestly striving to trace out what the sacred Scriptures teach, and following the views of the fathers, we believe that he who is from the root of Jesse, from the seed of David, born of a woman according to the flesh, who is with us under the law as a man and above us, above the law, as God, who for our sake and with us was among the dead, and who is above us, through himself life-giving and life itself, is truly the Son of God. We neither strip the humanity of the Godhead, nor divest the Word of humanity after the ineffable union. Rather, we confess one and the same Son, who has come forth inexpressibly from two realities into one being made of both, by the highest union, that is, and not by any change of nature. How great a gain awaits those who believe this, the disciple of Christ makes plain when he says: “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” And that Jesus Christ, who is from David according to the flesh, is by nature and truly the Son of God, inasmuch as the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, the wise John confirms when he says: “And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God; and we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.” Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
